entities.name: Prayer of Manasseh
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Prayer of Manasseh is a poignant and significant text attributed to King Manasseh of Judah, known for his tumultuous reign during the 7th century BCE. Composed in Greek around the 1st or 2nd century BCE, this 15-verse prayer is found in some versions of the Orthodox Deuterocanon, reflecting the penitential themes of repentance and divine mercy. It holds a crucial place in the history of Jewish and Christian liturgy, encapsulating the human struggle for forgiveness and redemption, which resonates across cultures and eras.

The text is traditionally believed to express the sincere penitence of King Manasseh, who, according to the Hebrew Bible, was infamous for idolatry and sin during his forty-five-year reign. The narrative details Manasseh's eventual turn toward God after being taken captive by the Assyrians, leading to his heartfelt plea for forgiveness. This moment is vital as it illustrates the themes of transformation and grace within the broader context of Judaic traditions and beliefs. The prayer serves as a bridge between the Hebrew Scriptures and later Christian adaptations, influencing religious thought and practice.

The legacy of the Prayer of Manasseh extends into both Jewish and Christian liturgical contexts, where it has been used in prayers and reflections on repentance. Its inclusion in various biblical canons demonstrates its lasting impact on religious communities and theological discussions about sin and redemption. The text has also influenced a diverse range of artistic and literary works, echoing the themes of repentance and divine mercy through centuries.

Notably, the prayer has been described as a profound articulation of the human condition, with its plea 'O Lord, I have sinned; I am sorry for my sins' encapsulating the universal quest for forgiveness. The enduring relevance of this text underscores its importance in both religious and historical discourse, as it continues to inspire believers striving for spiritual renewal.
